slides.title: Viewing Without A Magic Matrix
slides.notes: Open by making viewing a debugging story rather than a single matrix. The learner should leave the first slide expecting each transform to have a domain, a codomain, and an invariant. Mention the assigned source span, printed pages 157 through 176, only as orientation for the chapter coverage.

slides.title: The Route From Model To Pixels
slides.notes: Use the route map as the lecture contract. Each arrow has a different responsibility: modeling places objects, the camera changes coordinates, projection normalizes a view volume, and the viewport assigns pixel centers. This prevents the common mistake of blaming one matrix when the failure belongs to another stage.

slides.title: A Matrix Product Is A Contract
slides.notes: Emphasize that matrix order is not notation decoration. The rightmost matrix consumes the original world point, and each later matrix assumes the previous coordinate system has already been produced. Ask students to name the coordinate space before and after every multiplication in the product.

slides.title: Viewport As A Pixel Window Map
slides.notes: Explain the pixel-center convention before writing the matrix. The canonical square is continuous, but a raster image stores samples at pixel centers. Mapping -1 to -0.5 and 1 to nx minus 0.5 makes the visible image boundary align with the outer edges of the first and last pixels.

slides.title: Orthographic Box To Canonical Cube
slides.notes: Frame orthographic projection as the same windowing idea in three coordinates. Nothing about perspective is needed yet; the matrix merely recenters and rescales an axis-aligned view box. Stress the sign convention: in the right-handed camera setup, farther points usually have more negative z values.

slides.title: Camera Basis From Eye, Gaze, And Up
slides.notes: This is the most common source of viewing bugs. The inputs eye, gaze, and up do not automatically form an orthonormal frame. The construction turns gaze into the backward camera axis, removes the up-vector skew through a cross product, and then rebuilds a consistent right-handed basis.

slides.title: The Camera Matrix Is Translate Then Rotate
slides.notes: Separate the two jobs of the camera matrix. Translation moves the eye to the origin, while the basis rows measure coordinates along the camera axes. The eye must map to zero, and the basis rows must remain orthonormal; those two checks catch many sign and ordering errors.

slides.title: Homogeneous Coordinates Add A Denominator
slides.notes: Projective coordinates are the conceptual turn of the chapter. Affine transforms keep w equal to one, but viewing benefits from letting w change with depth. Only after the matrix product is finished do we divide by w to recover Cartesian coordinates for clipping and rasterization.

slides.title: Projective Maps Keep Lines Straight
slides.notes: Use the square-to-quadrilateral visual to separate what survives from what does not. Incidence and straightness survive under a projective map, while parallelism and midpoint ratios can change. This distinction prepares students for perspective images, where railroad tracks may meet but edges still draw as lines.

slides.title: Perspective Starts With A Frustum
slides.notes: The frustum diagram should be read from the eye outward. Points on the near plane keep their x and y positions after the perspective step, while the larger far rectangle is squeezed to match the orthographic box. That makes the later orthographic machinery reusable instead of special-casing perspective everywhere.

slides.title: Insert P Before The Orthographic Map
slides.notes: Keep the matrix ordering visible here. The perspective matrix P operates in camera coordinates, before the orthographic normalization and before the viewport. Once P has reshaped the frustum into a box, the same canonical-cube map and screen-window map can serve both projection styles.

slides.title: Depth Becomes Nonlinear But Ordered
slides.notes: Students often expect depth to be linear because x and y are easy to picture. The useful invariant is weaker and more important: inside a clipped view volume, nearer and farther points keep their order after the transform. The depth curve explains why z precision becomes concentrated near the eye.

slides.title: Lines Survive, Parameters Do Not
slides.notes: The line preservation claim is exact, but the sampling parameter is not preserved. A point halfway along a 3D segment can project away from the midpoint between projected endpoints. This is the reason interpolation in later pipeline stages must respect homogeneous coordinates rather than naive screen-space fractions.

slides.title: Field Of View Chooses The Near Window
slides.notes: Field of view is not an extra projection method. It is a compact way to compute the near-plane window before constructing the general perspective map. Increasing the vertical angle increases the window height through a tangent, and the aspect ratio expands width without changing the chosen vertical angle.

slides.title: Viewing Bugs Have Signatures
slides.notes: Use this slide as a diagnostic lab. A mirrored image points to a handedness or cross-product issue, a shifted image points to viewport or window bounds, clipped near objects suggest frustum signs, and w crossing zero warns that geometry needs clipping before the homogeneous divide.

slides.title: A Rendering Recipe For Wireframe Viewing
slides.notes: Walk through the recipe as executable thinking rather than API ceremony. Build camera axes, compose the projection and viewport matrices once, transform every endpoint, divide when required, reject or clip invalid segments, and finally draw in pixel coordinates. The order is what makes the implementation testable.

slides.title: Invariant Ledger
slides.notes: Close by revisiting the invariant ledger. Viewport corners, orthographic box corners, camera orthonormality, projective scale equivalence, perspective near and far corners, depth order, line preservation, and field-of-view formulas form a compact checklist for verifying a viewing implementation before adding rasterization details.
